menstrual-cycle.short: The roughly monthly cycle in which brain and ovarian hormones prepare the body for a possible pregnancy. Day 1 is the first day of bleeding. Research treats 21–35 days as normal.

ovulation.short: The release of an egg from an ovary, around the middle of a typical cycle. A surge of LH triggers it, and progesterone rises after it.

follicular-phase.short: The first half of the cycle: from the first day of bleeding until ovulation. Oestrogen rises and peaks just before ovulation; progesterone stays low.

luteal-phase.short: The second half of the cycle: from ovulation until the next bleed. Progesterone is high in the middle of it, and oestrogen is raised too.

progesterone.short: A steroid hormone made mostly after ovulation. It is low before ovulation and peaks about a week after it, in the middle of the luteal phase.

eumenorrhoea.short: A regular cycle of 21–35 days in which ovulation really happens. Regular bleeding alone does not prove it: ovulation and the hormone profile must be confirmed.

anovulatory-cycle.short: A cycle with bleeding but no ovulation, so progesterone never rises as it should. From the outside it can look regular.

ovulation-test.short: A home urine strip that detects the LH surge just before ovulation. Researchers use a positive result to time ovulation.

credible-interval.short: A range that, given the data, probably holds the true effect (often 95% likely). It plays the role of a confidence interval in Bayesian statistics. If it includes zero, 'no effect' is still plausible.

thermoregulation.short: How the body keeps its core temperature steady: sweating, widening skin blood vessels, shivering and changing behaviour.

hormonal-contraceptive.short: A method that prevents pregnancy with hormones: pill, implant, injection, hormonal coil (IUD), vaginal ring or patch. The copper coil has no hormones.

progestin.short: A man-made hormone that acts like progesterone. Contraceptives use it alone or together with a man-made oestrogen.

combined-pill.short: A contraceptive pill with both a man-made oestrogen and a progestin, usually taken on active days with a pill-free or placebo break.

withdrawal-bleed.short: The bleed in the pill-free or placebo days of the pill. It follows the drop in hormone dose, so it is not a true period.

postpartum.short: The time after giving birth. Research often counts the 12 months that follow.

pelvic-floor.short: The sling of muscles at the base of the pelvis that supports the bladder, womb and bowel. Pregnancy and birth can weaken it, and leaks when running are a warning sign.

lactation.short: Making breast milk. It costs energy and changes hormone levels.

perimenopause.short: The years around the menopause when the ovaries gradually make less oestrogen and cycles become irregular.

menopause.short: The time when menstruation stops for good. Post-menopause starts after 12 months without a period.

contraindication.short: A health condition that makes a treatment or activity unsafe, so it should be avoided (absolute) or only done after weighing risks with a doctor (relative).

instrumental-delivery.short: A birth in which the baby is helped out with forceps or a suction cup (vacuum).
